Aggregate end use load response on the day that sets the new system net load peak and the following two days. 3.2.2 Bill impacts The above load response to prices results in bills savings for customers. The total annual savings (per customer, for the given end use) is shown in Figure 18. The height of the bar represents the median savings across the customer clusters modeled, while error bars show the range (10th to 90th percentile) of results. In the residential sector, the largest savings potential comes from Level 2 EVs, followed by Level 1 EVs and pool pumps. For these year-round loads, the SDG&E price profile offers the most savings potential, as these customers prices are generally higher across the year. However, the thermal loads show similar results for PG&E and SDG&E savings potential. This could be either because the PG&E price profile has a shape that is more conducive to seasonal savings, or because customers in those territories tend to have larger thermal loads that lend themselves to higher savings. In all cases, bill savings significantly decline when moving from a Full, to Medium, to Mild tariff design. The flatter price shape of the Mild tariff offers less savings potential, which especially impacts the thermal loads that can only shift loads over relatively short time periods. With the flatter price shapes, the price differential for a consecutive 4- or 6-hour ramping period, over which these loads can be moved is going to be very limited. Nonetheless, customers are saving hundreds of dollars on price response in the majority of scenarios and end uses (space heating and all thermal loads on the Mild tariff being the primary exceptions). The range of results across a given end use are substantial, particularly for non-residential customers and for the Full and Medium tariff designs. In most cases, the customers with the most savings save twice as much as the median value, if not more, while other customers have very limited potential. This highlights the importance of targeting customers for adoption of these technologies and providing them with educational materials and tools to help them understand 32 their potential savings. Further, this distribution of savings potentials may present opportunities for programs that leverage customer surplus from high savers to support those customers that save less. Figure 18. Annual bill savings from price response for nine sector-end use combinations. The height of the colored bars shows the median bill savings for the given utility and tariff scenario, while the error bars show the range of results excluding the top and bottom 10%. End uses are exposed to different prices depending on their operational schedules. End uses that are more coincident with high prices, such as space cooling, will cost customers more on a per-kWh basis than other end uses. Similarly, end uses that are more flexible will be able to be operated at much lower average prices than those that cannot be flexed as much.
